Exact references: the square-root Kalman filter and the RTS smoother

An ensemble filter is an approximation, so it needs something exact to be measured against. For a linear-Gaussian state-space model that thing exists: the posterior is Gaussian, and its mean and covariance have a closed recursion Kalman, 1960Rauch et al., 1965. filterax ships two exact solvers for this case, filters.SquareRootKF and KalmanSmoother, and neither is an ensemble method.

Three ideas organise this chapter. On a linear-Gaussian model these two classes compute the posterior itself, which we check against a dense solve of the joint Gaussian. The square-root form carries a factor instead of a covariance, and it parallelises in time because the filter’s steps combine associatively. And an ensemble converges to these references at the rate 1/NE1 / \sqrt{N_\mathcal{E}}1/NE​​, which we measure.

What they compute¶

The model has a state xt∈RDx\vect{x}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}xt​∈RDx​ and observations yt∈RDy\vect{y}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y}yt​∈RDy​ for t=1,…,Tt = 1, \dots, Tt=1,…,T:

xt=Ftxt−1+ηt,yt=Htxt+εt,\vect{x}_t = \mat{F}_t \vect{x}_{t-1} + \gvect{\eta}_t, \qquad \vect{y}_t = \mat{H}_t \vect{x}_t + \gvect{\varepsilon}_t,xt​=Ft​xt−1​+ηt​,yt​=Ht​xt​+εt​,
(17.1)

with Ft∈RDx×Dx\mat{F}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}Ft​∈RDx​×Dx​, Ht∈RDy×Dx\mat{H}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y \times D_x}Ht​∈RDy​×Dx​, ηt∼N(0,Ση)\gvect{\eta}_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\vect{0}, \gmat{\Sigma}_\eta)ηt​∼N(0,Ση​) and εt∼N(0,Σε)\gvect{\varepsilon}_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\vect{0}, \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon)εt​∼N(0,Σε​). Write μx,t∣s∈RDx\gvect{\mu}_{x,t \mid s} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}μx,t∣s​∈RDx​ and Σx,t∣s∈RDx×Dx\gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t \mid s} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}Σx,t∣s​∈RDx​×Dx​ for the mean and covariance of xt\vect{x}_txt​ given y1:s\vect{y}_{1:s}y1:s​. The filter alternates a prediction and an update. With the residual rt∈RDy\vect{r}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y}rt​∈RDy​, the innovation covariance Σy,t\gmat{\Sigma}_{y,t}Σy,t​ and the gain Gt∈RDx×Dy\mat{G}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_y}Gt​∈RDx​×Dy​,

μx,t∣t−1=Ftμx,t−1∣t−1,Σx,t∣t−1=FtΣx,t−1∣t−1Ft⊤+Ση,\gvect{\mu}_{x,t \mid t-1} = \mat{F}_t \gvect{\mu}_{x,t-1 \mid t-1}, \qquad \gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t \mid t-1} = \mat{F}_t \gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t-1 \mid t-1} \mat{F}_t^\top + \gmat{\Sigma}_\eta,μx,t∣t−1​=Ft​μx,t−1∣t−1​,Σx,t∣t−1​=Ft​Σx,t−1∣t−1​Ft⊤​+Ση​,

rt=yt−Htμx,t∣t−1,Σy,t=HtΣx,t∣t−1Ht⊤+Σε,Gt=Σx,t∣t−1Ht⊤Σy,t−1,\vect{r}_t = \vect{y}_t - \mat{H}_t \gvect{\mu}_{x,t \mid t-1}, \qquad \gmat{\Sigma}_{y,t} = \mat{H}_t \gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t \mid t-1} \mat{H}_t^\top + \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon, \qquad \mat{G}_t = \gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t \mid t-1} \mat{H}_t^\top \gmat{\Sigma}_{y,t}^{-1},rt​=yt​−Ht​μx,t∣t−1​,Σy,t​=Ht​Σx,t∣t−1​Ht⊤​+Σε​,Gt​=Σx,t∣t−1​Ht⊤​Σy,t−1​,
(17.3)
μx,t∣t=μx,t∣t−1+Gtrt,Σx,t∣t=Σx,t∣t−1−GtΣy,tGt⊤.\gvect{\mu}_{x,t \mid t} = \gvect{\mu}_{x,t \mid t-1} + \mat{G}_t \vect{r}_t, \qquad \gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t \mid t} = \gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t \mid t-1} - \mat{G}_t \gmat{\Sigma}_{y,t} \mat{G}_t^\top.μx,t∣t​=μx,t∣t−1​+Gt​rt​,Σx,t∣t​=Σx,t∣t−1​−Gt​Σy,t​Gt⊤​.

The evidence is a by-product, since each residual is Gaussian given the past:

log⁡p(y1:T)=∑t=1Tlog⁡N(rt;0,Σy,t).\log p(\vect{y}_{1:T}) = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \log \mathcal{N}(\vect{r}_t; \vect{0}, \gmat{\Sigma}_{y,t}).logp(y1:T​)=t=1∑T​logN(rt​;0,Σy,t​).
(17.5)

The Rauch-Tung-Striebel pass Rauch et al., 1965 then runs backward from μx,T∣T\gvect{\mu}_{x,T \mid T}μx,T∣T​, with the smoother gain Gsmooth,t∈RDx×Dx\mat{G}_{\text{smooth},t} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}Gsmooth,t​∈RDx​×Dx​:

Gsmooth,t=Σx,t∣tFt+1⊤Σx,t+1∣t−1,\mat{G}_{\text{smooth},t} = \gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t \mid t} \mat{F}_{t+1}^\top \gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t+1 \mid t}^{-1},Gsmooth,t​=Σx,t∣t​Ft+1⊤​Σx,t+1∣t−1​,
(17.6)
μx,t∣T=μx,t∣t+Gsmooth,t(μx,t+1∣T−μx,t+1∣t),\gvect{\mu}_{x,t \mid T} = \gvect{\mu}_{x,t \mid t} + \mat{G}_{\text{smooth},t} (\gvect{\mu}_{x,t+1 \mid T} - \gvect{\mu}_{x,t+1 \mid t}),μx,t∣T​=μx,t∣t​+Gsmooth,t​(μx,t+1∣T​−μx,t+1∣t​),
(17.7)
Σx,t∣T=Σx,t∣t+Gsmooth,t(Σx,t+1∣T−Σx,t+1∣t)Gsmooth,t⊤.\gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t \mid T} = \gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t \mid t} + \mat{G}_{\text{smooth},t} (\gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t+1 \mid T} - \gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t+1 \mid t}) \mat{G}_{\text{smooth},t}^\top.Σx,t∣T​=Σx,t∣t​+Gsmooth,t​(Σx,t+1∣T​−Σx,t+1∣t​)Gsmooth,t⊤​.
(17.8)

Nothing here is estimated, and no sampling enters. So on a linear-Gaussian model the error of an ensemble method against these numbers is the error of the ensemble method, which is what makes them a reference. Outside that model they are not the posterior, and chapter 20 needs a grid instead.

The two classes¶

The classes differ in more than their names.

filters.SquareRootKFKalmanSmoother
Returnsfiltered and predicted marginals, log⁡p(y1:T)\log p(\vect{y}_{1:T})logp(y1:T​)filtered and smoothed marginals, log⁡p(y1:T)\log p(\vect{y}_{1:T})logp(y1:T​)
Solvergaussx.parallel_kalman_filter(square_root=True)gaussx.kalman_filter, then gaussx.rts_smoother
Formfactors, in an associative scan over timecovariances, sequential in time
Priorone transition before y1\vect{y}_1y1​at the time of y1\vect{y}_1y1​, so T−1T - 1T−1 transitions
Modelone F\mat{F}F, H\mat{H}H, Ση\gmat{\Sigma}_\etaΣη​, Σε\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilonΣε​ for all timesa stack over time, or one for all times
Missing datanone in the wrappera (T, D_y) mask, with NaN allowed at masked entries
Irregular timesnoKalmanSmoother.from_sde

SquareRootFilterResult holds filtered_means, filtered_covs, predicted_means, predicted_covs and log_likelihood. KalmanSmoothingResult holds filtered_means, filtered_covs, smoothed_means, smoothed_covs and log_likelihood, and it keeps no cross-time covariances.

The prior convention is the difference most likely to catch you out. To make the two agree, start KalmanSmoother from the one-step prediction of the SquareRootKF prior, N(Fμx,0,FΣx,0F⊤+Ση)\mathcal{N}(\mat{F} \gvect{\mu}_{x,0}, \mat{F} \gmat{\Sigma}_{x,0} \mat{F}^\top + \gmat{\Sigma}_\eta)N(Fμx,0​,FΣx,0​F⊤+Ση​).

Program 17.1 runs both on the same model, with Dx=3D_x = 3Dx​=3, Dy=2D_y = 2Dy​=2 and T=40T = 40T=40, on data drawn from the model. It compares them with two references that use no filter code at all. One is a dense Joseph-form recursion for (17.4). The other is one conditioning of the joint Gaussian of (x1:T,y1:T)(\vect{x}_{1:T}, \vect{y}_{1:T})(x1:T​,y1:T​), whose state block has side TDxT D_xTDx​.

It prints 6e-15, 2e-15, 1e-14, 6e-15, 3e-13, 2e-14 and 7e-13. The first three compare SquareRootKF with the Joseph-form filter, on the means, the covariances and the log-likelihood. The fourth compares the filtered means of the two classes. The last three compare KalmanSmoother with the dense joint solve, on the smoothed means, the smoothed covariances and the log-likelihood. All seven are float64 round-off, so the classes compute the posterior and not an approximation to it.

Irregular times and missing data¶

KalmanSmoother does not need a time grid. KalmanSmoother.from_sde takes a gaussx SDE kernel and discretises it over the actual gaps Δτt=τt−τt−1\Delta \tau_t = \tau_t - \tau_{t-1}Δτt​=τt​−τt−1​ between the time stamps τt\tau_tτt​:

Ft=exp⁡(AΔτt),Ση,t=Σx,∞−FtΣx,∞Ft⊤,\mat{F}_t = \exp(\mat{A} \Delta \tau_t), \qquad \gmat{\Sigma}_{\eta,t} = \gmat{\Sigma}_{x,\infty} - \mat{F}_t \gmat{\Sigma}_{x,\infty} \mat{F}_t^\top,Ft​=exp(AΔτt​),Ση,t​=Σx,∞​−Ft​Σx,∞​Ft⊤​,
(17.9)

where A\mat{A}A is the drift of the SDE and Σx,∞\gmat{\Sigma}_{x,\infty}Σx,∞​ its stationary covariance, which is also the prior of x1\vect{x}_1x1​. A Matérn kernel has such a form, and then the smoothed mean is Gaussian process regression. So Program 17.2 has a reference with no state space in it at all: a dense GP solve with the Matérn-3/2 kernel, at 30 irregular times, one of which is masked. The masked entry is NaN, which the class never reads.

A mask makes an entry inert. Its row of Ht\mat{H}_tHt​ is zeroed, its row and column of Σε,t\gmat{\Sigma}_{\varepsilon,t}Σε,t​ become those of the identity, and its datum becomes 0. Then Σy,t\gmat{\Sigma}_{y,t}Σy,t​ splits into a block for the observed entries and an identity block for the rest. So that column of the gain vanishes, and the update equals the one with the entry deleted.

It prints 3e-15, 8e-16 and 9e-15, for the smoothed mean, the smoothed variance and the log-likelihood. A filter over 30 irregular times and a dense GP solve therefore give the same answer, with the masked time contributing nothing to the evidence.

The square-root form¶

The covariance form of (17.4) subtracts, so rounding can push Σx,t∣t\gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t \mid t}Σx,t∣t​ out of the positive semi-definite cone. A square-root filter carries a factor Lx\mat{L}_xLx​ with Σx=LxLx⊤\gmat{\Sigma}_x = \mat{L}_x \mat{L}_x^\topΣx​=Lx​Lx⊤​ instead, so the covariance it reports is a Gram matrix.

Call tria(A)\op{tria}(\mat{A})tria(A) the lower-triangular L\mat{L}L with LL⊤=AA⊤\mat{L} \mat{L}^\top = \mat{A} \mat{A}^\topLL⊤=AA⊤, which is the transpose of the R\mat{R}R in a QR decomposition of A⊤\mat{A}^\topA⊤. Prediction stacks the two factors of (17.2) side by side:

Lx,t∣t−1=tria([FtLx,t−1∣t−1Lη]).\mat{L}_{x,t \mid t-1} = \op{tria}\big(\begin{bmatrix} \mat{F}_t \mat{L}_{x,t-1 \mid t-1} & \mat{L}_\eta \end{bmatrix}\big).Lx,t∣t−1​=tria([Ft​Lx,t−1∣t−1​​Lη​​]).
(17.10)

The update gets everything from one triangularisation. With Lx=Lx,t∣t−1\mat{L}_x = \mat{L}_{x,t \mid t-1}Lx​=Lx,t∣t−1​, and Ψ∈R(Dy+Dx)×(Dy+Dx)\gmat{\Psi} \in \mathbb{R}^{(D_y + D_x) \times (D_y + D_x)}Ψ∈R(Dy​+Dx​)×(Dy​+Dx​) partitioned into blocks,

Ψ=tria[HLxLεLx0]=[Ψ110Ψ21Ψ22].\gmat{\Psi} = \op{tria} \begin{bmatrix} \mat{H} \mat{L}_x & \mat{L}_\varepsilon \\ \mat{L}_x & \mat{0} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \gmat{\Psi}_{11} & \mat{0} \\ \gmat{\Psi}_{21} & \gmat{\Psi}_{22} \end{bmatrix}.Ψ=tria[HLx​Lx​​Lε​0​]=[Ψ11​Ψ21​​0Ψ22​​].
(17.11)

Multiplying the stacked matrix by its transpose gives

ΨΨ⊤=[ΣyHΣxΣxH⊤Σx].\gmat{\Psi} \gmat{\Psi}^\top = \begin{bmatrix} \gmat{\Sigma}_y & \mat{H} \gmat{\Sigma}_x \\ \gmat{\Sigma}_x \mat{H}^\top & \gmat{\Sigma}_x \end{bmatrix}.ΨΨ⊤=[Σy​Σx​H⊤​HΣx​Σx​​].
(17.12)

Reading (17.12) block by block gives each quantity by hand. The top left says Ψ11Ψ11⊤=Σy\gmat{\Psi}_{11} \gmat{\Psi}_{11}^\top = \gmat{\Sigma}_yΨ11​Ψ11⊤​=Σy​, so Ψ11=Ly\gmat{\Psi}_{11} = \mat{L}_yΨ11​=Ly​. The bottom right says Ψ21Ψ21⊤+Ψ22Ψ22⊤=Σx\gmat{\Psi}_{21} \gmat{\Psi}_{21}^\top + \gmat{\Psi}_{22} \gmat{\Psi}_{22}^\top = \gmat{\Sigma}_xΨ21​Ψ21⊤​+Ψ22​Ψ22⊤​=Σx​, and Ψ21Ψ21⊤=GΣyG⊤\gmat{\Psi}_{21} \gmat{\Psi}_{21}^\top = \mat{G} \gmat{\Sigma}_y \mat{G}^\topΨ21​Ψ21⊤​=GΣy​G⊤, so

(17.13)

No covariance is formed and nothing subtracts.

Combining steps in parallel¶

The recursion looks sequential, but the steps combine associatively Särkkä & Garcı́a-Fernández, 2021, and so they can run as a parallel scan. Take a block of steps from sss to uuu. Describe it by what it says about the state at its end given the state at its start, and about the data in between:

p(xu∣xs,ys+1:u)=N(xu;Fcondxs+μcond,Σcond),p(\vect{x}_u \mid \vect{x}_s, \vect{y}_{s+1:u}) = \mathcal{N}(\vect{x}_u; \mat{F}_\text{cond} \vect{x}_s + \gvect{\mu}_\text{cond}, \gmat{\Sigma}_\text{cond}),p(xu​∣xs​,ys+1:u​)=N(xu​;Fcond​xs​+μcond​,Σcond​),
(17.14)
p(ys+1:u∣xs)∝exp⁡(−12xs⊤Λlikxs+blik⊤xs).p(\vect{y}_{s+1:u} \mid \vect{x}_s) \propto \exp\big(-\tfrac{1}{2} \vect{x}_s^\top \gmat{\Lambda}_\text{lik} \vect{x}_s + \vect{b}_\text{lik}^\top \vect{x}_s\big).p(ys+1:u​∣xs​)∝exp(−21​xs⊤​Λlik​xs​+blik⊤​xs​).
(17.15)

These five quantities, with Fcond,Σcond,Λlik∈RDx×Dx\mat{F}_\text{cond}, \gmat{\Sigma}_\text{cond}, \gmat{\Lambda}_\text{lik} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}Fcond​,Σcond​,Λlik​∈RDx​×Dx​ and μcond,blik∈RDx\gvect{\mu}_\text{cond}, \vect{b}_\text{lik} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}μcond​,blik​∈RDx​, are an element. For one step t≥2t \ge 2t≥2 they are the update of (17.4) with Ση\gmat{\Sigma}_\etaΣη​ as the predicted covariance. With Σy∣x=HtΣηHt⊤+Σε\gmat{\Sigma}_{y \mid x} = \mat{H}_t \gmat{\Sigma}_\eta \mat{H}_t^\top + \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilonΣy∣x​=Ht​Ση​Ht⊤​+Σε​ and Gcond=ΣηHt⊤Σy∣x−1\mat{G}_\text{cond} = \gmat{\Sigma}_\eta \mat{H}_t^\top \gmat{\Sigma}_{y \mid x}^{-1}Gcond​=Ση​Ht⊤​Σy∣x−1​,

Fcond=(I−GcondHt)Ft,μcond=Gcondyt,Σcond=(I−GcondHt)Ση,\mat{F}_\text{cond} = (\mat{I} - \mat{G}_\text{cond} \mat{H}_t) \mat{F}_t, \qquad \gvect{\mu}_\text{cond} = \mat{G}_\text{cond} \vect{y}_t, \qquad \gmat{\Sigma}_\text{cond} = (\mat{I} - \mat{G}_\text{cond} \mat{H}_t) \gmat{\Sigma}_\eta,Fcond​=(I−Gcond​Ht​)Ft​,μcond​=Gcond​yt​,Σcond​=(I−Gcond​Ht​)Ση​,
(17.16)

The first step absorbs the prior instead: its Fcond\mat{F}_\text{cond}Fcond​, blik\vect{b}_\text{lik}blik​ and Λlik\gmat{\Lambda}_\text{lik}Λlik​ are zero, and its μcond\gvect{\mu}_\text{cond}μcond​ and Σcond\gmat{\Sigma}_\text{cond}Σcond​ are the filtered moments at t=1t = 1t=1.

To join a block iii from sss to uuu with a block jjj from uuu to vvv, integrate out xu\vect{x}_uxu​. That Gaussian integral gives

(17.20)

with the subscript cond or lik dropped. The first element has Fcond=0\mat{F}_\text{cond} = \mat{0}Fcond​=0, so every prefix that starts at it has Fij=0\mat{F}_{ij} = \mat{0}Fij​=0. The μ\gvect{\mu}μ and Σ\gmat{\Sigma}Σ of such a prefix are the filtered moments at its end. So an associative scan returns all TTT filtered marginals, with O(log⁡T)O(\log T)O(logT) span given enough processors.

The square-root form of Yaghoobi et al. (2025) carries Lcond\mat{L}_\text{cond}Lcond​ and Llik\mat{L}_\text{lik}Llik​ with Σcond=LcondLcond⊤\gmat{\Sigma}_\text{cond} = \mat{L}_\text{cond} \mat{L}_\text{cond}^\topΣcond​=Lcond​Lcond⊤​ and Λlik=LlikLlik⊤\gmat{\Lambda}_\text{lik} = \mat{L}_\text{lik} \mat{L}_\text{lik}^\topΛlik​=Llik​Llik⊤​. Each combination triangularises a stack holding an identity,

Ξ=tria[Li⊤Llik,jI],M=LiΞ−⊤,MM⊤=(I+ΣiΛj)−1Σi,\gmat{\Xi} = \op{tria} \begin{bmatrix} \mat{L}_i^\top \mat{L}_{\text{lik},j} & \mat{I} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mat{M} = \mat{L}_i \gmat{\Xi}^{-\top}, \qquad \mat{M} \mat{M}^\top = (\mat{I} + \gmat{\Sigma}_i \gmat{\Lambda}_j)^{-1} \gmat{\Sigma}_i,Ξ=tria[Li⊤​Llik,j​​I​],M=Li​Ξ−⊤,MM⊤=(I+Σi​Λj​)−1Σi​,
(17.21)

where Ξ,M∈RDx×Dx\gmat{\Xi}, \mat{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}Ξ,M∈RDx​×Dx​. The factor of (17.19) is then Lij=tria([FjM,Lj])\mat{L}_{ij} = \op{tria}([\mat{F}_j \mat{M}, \mat{L}_j])Lij​=tria([Fj​M,Lj​]). gaussx.parallel_kalman_filter(square_root=True) does exactly this, and SquareRootKF is a thin wrapper around it that reports the covariances LL⊤\mat{L} \mat{L}^\topLL⊤. The model covariances are factored once, outside the scan, by a Cholesky of their correlation matrix. That follows a diagonal shift of 4Dϵ4 D \epsilon4Dϵ, with DDD the matrix’s side and ϵ\epsilonϵ the machine epsilon, so a covariance that is singular only by rounding still factors.

Algorithm¶

Program 17.3 writes this out in dense numpy for the model above. It builds the TTT elements, reduces them from the left and in a balanced tree, and takes one update through (17.11). The two reductions must agree with each other, and with the last filtered moments of SquareRootKF, because the operation is associative and the elements describe the same posterior.

It prints 2e-15 2e-16, 6e-15, 2e-15, 3e-16 and 2e-16. The first pair says the two reductions agree on the last mean and covariance. The next two say they match SquareRootKF, and the last two say the update by triangularisation matches the Joseph form.

Float32 and strong observations¶

The point of a factor is what happens in float32, and the test of it is the mean. A covariance can be positive definite while the mean beside it is wrong, and this is not a hypothetical. Before gaussx v0.6.9 the means of square_root=True were up to billions of standard deviations off on the models below, while the covariances still looked healthy, as tests/test_filters_advanced.py records.

The cause was the mean shift of (17.18). The push-through identity gives (I+ΣiΛj)−1v=v−MM⊤Λjv(\mat{I} + \gmat{\Sigma}_i \gmat{\Lambda}_j)^{-1} \vect{v} = \vect{v} - \mat{M} \mat{M}^\top \gmat{\Lambda}_j \vect{v}(I+Σi​Λj​)−1v=v−MM⊤Λj​v, which subtracts nearly equal vectors when ΣiΛj\gmat{\Sigma}_i \gmat{\Lambda}_jΣi​Λj​ is near 1/ϵ1 / \epsilon1/ϵ. Applied to v=Σibj\vect{v} = \gmat{\Sigma}_i \vect{b}_jv=Σi​bj​, a large vector, the rounding swamps the answer. By (17.21) the same quantity has a form with nothing to cancel:

(I+ΣiΛj)−1Σibj=MM⊤bj.(\mat{I} + \gmat{\Sigma}_i \gmat{\Lambda}_j)^{-1} \gmat{\Sigma}_i \vect{b}_j = \mat{M} \mat{M}^\top \vect{b}_j.(I+Σi​Λj​)−1Σi​bj​=MM⊤bj​.
(17.22)

gaussx uses this for the shift and keeps the push-through only for μi\gvect{\mu}_iμi​. Chapter 18 measures the two forms side by side.

Program 17.4 runs the constant-velocity model of those tests, with T=64T = 64T=64 and data drawn from the model, against float64 SquareRootKF as the reference. It reports the largest mean error in reference standard deviations, the log-likelihood error, and the smallest eigenvalue of the filtered covariances.

It prints the following, where sqrt is SquareRootKF, cov is the covariance form of gaussx.parallel_kalman_filter and seq is KalmanSmoother, which is also in covariance form:

Ση\gmat{\Sigma}_\etaΣη​, Σε\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilonΣε​, Σx,0\gmat{\Sigma}_{x,0}Σx,0​FormLargest mean error (sd)Log-likelihood errorSmallest eigenvalue

The variances are multiples of the identity, and the reference log-likelihoods are 329.432, 472.193 and 610.348. In float64 the two families agree to 6e-11, 4e-09 and 2e-06 standard deviations, so the reference does not depend on the form.

The factor pays for itself on the first two rows, with mean errors 5 to 35 times smaller than the covariance forms. It is also the only form that stays positive definite throughout. It is not exact, though. On the last row its means are 4.3 standard deviations off, and tests/test_filters_advanced.py only bounds that error by 10. There the sequential filter’s means are closer, even though its covariance is indefinite and its log-likelihood is NaN. So at that conditioning use float64 for a reference, whichever form you choose.

The ensemble against the reference¶

An ensemble filter on this model has no bias from nonlinearity, so what remains is sampling error, which should fall as 1/NE1 / \sqrt{N_\mathcal{E}}1/NE​​. Program 17.5 measures it. Each member takes its own draw of ηt\gvect{\eta}_tηt​ in the forecast, then filters.ETKF or filters.StochasticEnKF assimilates, and EnKS runs the backward pass. The numbers are averages over 6 independent runs of the RMS difference from the reference over all components and all T=40T = 40T=40 times.

It prints the mean error and the covariance error for each filter and its smoother, with the absolute error in the summed log-likelihood:

The last line it prints is -0.55, the slope of log error against log NEN_\mathcal{E}NE​ for the ETKF filter mean, close to the −1/2-1/2−1/2 that sampling error predicts. Each fourfold increase in members about halves the error columns, and the evidence error falls at least as fast, so no bias shows at these sizes. The stochastic filter adds observation perturbations on top of the sampled model noise. On this model that costs little: 0.210 against 0.204 at NE=40N_\mathcal{E} = 40NE​=40.

Read the other way, this sets a tolerance for a test: at NE=640N_\mathcal{E} = 640NE​=640 on this model a correct filter sits about 0.05 from the reference.

When it breaks¶

The references are exact for one model class, and they can fail you in the ways below.

  • Nonlinear or non-Gaussian. SquareRootKF and KalmanSmoother take matrices, so a nonlinear model has no entry point, and the ensemble methods then have no exact reference. Use a grid, as in chapter 20.

  • Scale. The cost is O(T(Dx3+Dy3))O(T (D_x^3 + D_y^3))O(T(Dx3​+Dy3​)) with dense Dx×DxD_x \times D_xDx​×Dx​ matrices, which is why they are references for small problems and not solvers for large ones.

  • Float32 at extreme conditioning. The table above shows every form losing the mean by the last row.

  • What the wrapper leaves out. SquareRootKF has one F\mat{F}F, H\mat{H}H, Ση\gmat{\Sigma}_\etaΣη​ and Σε\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilonΣε​ for all times and no mask. For either, call gaussx.parallel_kalman_filter directly.

  • The prior convention. Giving both classes the same prior is the mistake to expect, and Program 17.6 measures it.

It prints 0.037 7e-04 and 0.171. The filtered mean is off by 0.037 at the first time and the model has nearly forgotten it by the last, while the log-likelihood stays off by 0.171. Nothing raises, since both priors are valid.

When the exact references are the right answer¶

Use them when the model is linear and Gaussian and you want the answer rather than an estimate of it. That covers the baseline of a twin experiment, the ground truth of a test for a new filter, and a Gaussian process in time at O(T)O(T)O(T) through from_sde. Use SquareRootKF when the covariance must stay positive definite in float32, or when gaussx.parallel_kalman_filter’s scan suits your hardware. Use KalmanSmoother when you need smoothed marginals, missing data or irregular times.

Reach for an ensemble method when the model is nonlinear or DxD_xDx​ is too large for a dense matrix.
